submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole is a word-form detector for one family of common English relation words: the placement verbs lay/laid/laying/lays, lie/lies/lying, sit/sits/sitting/sat and put/puts/putting; the consequence adverbs thus, therefore and hence; the Latin conjunction et (chiefly in 'et al.'); the restatement adverbs merely, simply, basically, literally, namely and respectively; and, more weakly, the quantity/composition words sum, measure(s), consist(s), comprise(s) and discrete. It is form-specific rather than a semantic field: differently spelled near-synonyms (place, stand, rest, remain, set; however, moreover, clearly, obviously, generally, really, only) leave the pole at baseline in every context, so a text is predicted active iff it contains one of the listed word forms (or the tokenizer piece of one, e.g. ' lay' in 'layering', ' sit' in 'sitagliptin', 'ence' in 'Hence', ' pe' in 'pea'), with a line-initial occurrence attenuated.

OBC (One Bit Converter) is an hardware emulation inspired by the Motorola MC3518, single bit converters family. It converts digital signal to digital signal by using the single bit conversion emulation.
Principle of single bit conversion
The converter tries to follow an input signal (sample values) by adding or subtracting fixed values.
If the current output sample value is lower than the next input sample value, then an increment value is added to the next output value.
If the current output sample value is higher than the next input sample value, then a decrement value is subtracted to the next output value.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The harbor at Kestrel Bay has needed dredging for more than a decade. Sand and gravel wash down from the two creeks north of town, and every winter storm pushes another band of sediment into the channel. By March the deepest berth is barely deep enough for the fishing fleet, and the ferry that carries freight to the outer islands has to wait offshore for high water. Last autumn the town board asked a coastal engineering firm to survey the channel and report on options. The firm's draft, circulated in January, described three approaches: a long mechanical dig with a clamshell crane, a seasonal programme that clears a narrow path each spring, and a permanent stone wall that would steer the current away from the berth. The consultants recommended the seasonal programme as the cheapest and least disruptive, though they warned that it would need repeating every year and that the price would rise with fuel costs. Ratepayers were not pleased. At a crowded hearing in the school gym, several speakers argued that a permanent wall was the honest answer, while others said the whole exercise was a way to postpone a decision until after the next election. One fisherman pointed out that the fleet had lost eleven days of work the previous season and could not absorb another spring of waiting. A retired teacher asked why the board had waited until the berths were nearly unusable before ordering a survey at all. The board's chair, who has held the seat for six years, defended the timetable. She said the engineering firm had been chosen through a competitive process and that the draft had arrived within the agreed cost and schedule. She also noted that the wall option carried an environmental review that could take two or three years, and that the state agency responsible for the estuary had already signalled doubts about any hard structure in the channel. The firm's lead engineer, speaking after her, agreed that the wall was the most durable answer but added that it would shift erosion further downstream, where several private docks stand on pilings. Those owners, he said, had not been consulted and would likely object. He proposed a compromise: a seasonal dig for the next three years, with a portion of the annual cost set aside for a full wall design, so that the board could revisit the question once the design and permits were ready. That proposal carried by a single vote. The board directed the engineer to prepare bid documents before the end of April so that work could begin after the ferry schedule eased in June. It also created a small reserve, funded by a surcharge on mooring fees, to pay for the wall study. Whether the compromise will hold is unclear. The fishing fleet wants faster action; the dock owners want assurances that any wall will not worsen the current at their pilings; and the state agency has asked for a monitoring plan that the town has not yet paid for. The engineer's report closes with a warning that the channel will keep filling no matter which option the board chooses, and that the cost of doing nothing will be paid, sooner or later, by whoever needs to use the harbor. The town has basically bought itself three more years to argue.
